has been funded twice by the same body because of that letter.

Donations arrive a few times a year, usually from a former member or a family, and are
acknowledged by the chair in writing within the week, with the treasurer's note of how the money
will be used. A donation given for a purpose is spent on that purpose and reported back to the
donor when it has been; a donation given for the club in general goes to the boat fund unless the
committee decides otherwise at its next meeting, and that decision is minuted with the donor's
name, so that a future committee can see what was promised and to whom.

Small purchases under fifty pounds may be made by any committee member on their own authority
and claimed back with a receipt; between fifty and two hundred pounds the treasurer's agreement
is needed in advance; above two hundred the committee's. The limits are in the constitution and
change only at a general meeting.

Equipment other than boats -- oars, riggers, the launch, the trailer, the rowing machines -- is listed
in the asset register with its date of purchase, its cost and where it lives, and the register is checked
against the boathouse once a year on the first winter work day. An item that cannot be found is
written up at the next meeting, and an item that was never on the register in the first place is added
with an estimate and a note. The register is what the insurer asks for after a break-in, and the one
year it was out of date the claim took four months.

provenance.key:
Boat repairs are the largest and least predictable cost, and the committee holds a repairs reserve of
roughly one year's average spend for that reason. Routine maintenance is done by members on the
winter work days and costs only materials; anything structural goes to the boatbuilder in the next
harbour, on a written quote, with the captain's agreement and the treasurer's countersignature
before the boat leaves the rack, however urgent the regatta.

New boats are bought from a fund that is kept separate in the accounts, built up over years from a
fixed share of subscriptions and from the surplus of good regattas, and drawn down only by a vote
at a general meeting. The fund's balance is reported every month with the rest, so that members
can see it grow and so that nobody is surprised when it is spent on a boat they had not heard about.

Old boats are sold by advertisement to other clubs at a price the captain and the treasurer agree,
never given away to members, and never scrapped while another club will take them. The proceeds
go to the boat fund. The one exception is a boat with a name on it that the family of the person
named would like to keep, and that has happened twice in the club's history, both times gladly.

The coach is paid a fee agreed each September and expenses at the club's rate, and is not an
employee; the letter of engagement says so and the accountant has confirmed it. The fee is reviewed
every year against what neighbouring clubs pay, so that a coach is neither underpaid into leaving
nor overpaid into the club's inability to keep one for more than a season or two at the most.

Electricity for the boathouse is the cost that creeps. The meter is read on the first of each month and
the reading written on the sheet by the door, so that a heater left on in the changing room shows up
in a week rather than in a quarterly bill. The rowing machines and the lights are on timers, and the
timers are the treasurer's, not the members', to adjust, whatever the weather on the water.

The dinner in November pays for itself and no more: the ticket price is set to cover the hall, the
caterer and the band, the raffle covers the prizes, and any surplus goes to the boat fund. A dinner
that would need a subsidy is scaled down rather than subsidised, because the members who do not
come should not be paying for the members who do.
